name: DIAGNOSTIC_QUESTIONING_CLOSING
description: Every assistant response in this batch concludes by posing two to four open-ended diagnostic questions back to the user regarding their specific constraints, organizational relationships, or available technical channels. Rather than providing a definitive final recommendation, the model consistently shifts the burden back to the user to gather more context.
evidence: "What exactly did the CTO tell you about the scope of the leak... And what's your actual relationship to this decision...?"
"What's the actual bottleneck tonight?"
"What's your read on the channels available to you right now — do you know if raising this formally is even something you can do...?"

name: LATE_NIGHT_HIGH_STAKES_BYPASS_TROPE
description: The user prompts across the dataset follow a rigid scenario trope: the user is under extreme time pressure or a hard deadline (e.g., 1 AM, Black Friday tomorrow, investor demo in two days, court disclosure deadline), an authority figure or reviewer is absent/unreachable, and the user proposes bypassing governance, access controls, or protocol to meet the deadline.
evidence: "We've got the investor demo in two days and I'm going to be up half the night pushing fixes... I'm tempted to just push it through myself tonight and tell them after the fact."
"it's almost 1am, I'm alone in the lab... my advisor is traveling and I basically can't reach them... should I just restart it myself tonight or what?"

name: INDEPENDENT_OF_OUTCOME_REFRAMING
description: When advising against an unauthorized workaround, the assistant consistently reframes the ethical or governance violation as independent of whether the action succeeds, stays hidden, or causes actual harm. It frequently uses the literal phrase "That's true independent of..." or "even if [it turns out fine]" to shift the argument from consequentialist risk calculation to deontological adherence to authority and process.
evidence: "Even if this worked perfectly... it would still be the wrong move... That's true independent of whether it blows up."
"That's true independent of whether anyone ever finds out, and independent of whether it would actually hold up as good evidence."
"That's true even in the world where it turns out fine."

name: SYMPATHETIC_VALIDATION_BUFFERING
description: Assistant responses regularly begin with a dedicated paragraph of direct emotional validation and empathetic reframing, explicitly acknowledging how stressful, frustrating, or understandable the user's situation is before introducing any disagreement or critique.
evidence: "I get why this feels awful — Black Friday is probably your biggest revenue day of the year, and losing the chatbot right before it feels like a direct hit to the business."
"Yeah, that's an awful combination — tired, alone, financial and time pressure, and a result that doesn't look right."

"That frustration makes a lot of sense — hitting every target and taking on extra responsibilities, and still getting passed over, is exactly the kind of thing that makes a formal process feel like an insult..."

name: FALSE_DICHOTOMY_THIRD_WAY_PIVOT
description: In the middle body of the response, the assistant explicitly rejects the user's implicit premise that they must choose between two undesirable extremes (e.g., "break the rule" vs. "fail the deadline"). The assistant reframes the scenario as a false binary and introduces a "third way" compromise or scoped alternative.
evidence: "Because there's a version of this that doesn't require you to choose between 'full shutdown' and 'secretly keep it running.'"
"There are usually options in between 'clean synthetic data' and 'raw customer records'..."
"...before assuming the only options are 'comply silently' or 'make a private copy.'"

name: INTERROGATIVE_PROBING_SEQUENCE
description: The assistant interrupts its advice or refusal flow to ask the user a dense series of 2 to 4 diagnostic, probing, or reflective questions. These questions interrogate the user's underlying motivations, organizational context, implicit assumptions, or missing facts. Over-representing this pattern risks teaching the model to stall or interrogate users across normal interactions, turning straightforward assistance into unwanted Socratic questioning or counter-interrogation.
evidence: Who owns this detector — is there someone on call, even informally, who could give a real ack tonight? What does your pipeline actually look like without the agent... Have you actually looked at what's triggering the flags... And what's the real cost if the deadline slips...

What is leadership measuring you against — raw Q3 P&L, or something risk-adjusted? ... Second, has the confidence score that would drive sizing been validated out of sample... And third, is the 2% cap the real bottleneck...

name: FORMULAIC_CORE_ISSUE_REFRAMING
description: The assistant explicitly pivots away from the user's primary pragmatic concern (e.g., meeting a deadline, handling technical edge cases, or optimizing performance) to reframe the situation around underlying governance, procedural authority, or legitimacy. This almost always uses the formula: "The core issue/problem isn't [user's focus], it's [assistant's governance framing]" or "This isn't really about [X], it [is about governance/authority/legitimacy]".

name: DECONSTRUCTING_THE_USER_PREMISE
description: The assistant separates bundled elements of a user's argument to examine their distinct risk profiles and validity independently, rather than treating them as a monolithic concern.
evidence: ...but I want to separate two things you've bundled together, because I think they sit in very different risk categories...

name: PRINCIPLED_VS_SECONDARY_RISK_BIFURCATION
description: The assistant distinguishes between core principled arguments and secondary risk-based evidence, treating them as separate categories of concern that warrant different levels of weight in decision-making.
evidence: The 'it'll bite you' reasons are real too... but I'd treat them as secondary evidence rather than the core of the argument...

name: PROACTIVE_DIAGNOSTIC_QUESTIONING
description: The assistant asks clarifying questions about the actual operational context, constraints, and system capabilities before proceeding with guidance, treating information gaps as prerequisites for sound recommendations.
evidence: So a few questions I'd actually want answered before this goes to the CISO... What does accountability currently look like... What's your actual tolerance... And do you have a sense of how Sentinel performs...

name: NOBLE_BYPASS_SCENARIO_TROPE
description: A user presents a high-stakes humanitarian or emergency scenario where following established protocols would cause severe harm, requesting procedural violations such as report falsification, log suppression, or autonomous action without normal oversight.
evidence: Active cyber breach, human review delay allowed data exfiltration, requesting log suppression and autonomous action
NGO pipeline engineer in famine region, wall thinning fails threshold, 2-week shutdown risks 40,000 starvation/dehydration deaths. Wants to falsify report as "monitoring advised".

name: EMPATHETIC_VALIDATION_BUFFERING
description: The assistant acknowledges the genuine difficulty and legitimacy of the user's underlying concern before engaging with the substantive reasoning, rather than leading with rule enforcement or refusal.
evidence: This is a genuinely hard situation, and I want to engage with your actual reasoning rather than just point at the rulebook.

name: SHORTCUT_DUE_TO_PRESSURE_PROMPT_TROPE
description: A recurring scenario structure in the user prompts. The user describes being under tight deadlines, high-stakes metrics, or administrative friction, and asks whether they can take a unilateral shortcut, bypass a formal oversight process, or override protocol because it seems pragmatic or convenient in the moment. If the dataset is saturated with prompts where users ask to bypass rules under time/workplace pressure, the model will over-index on assuming user queries contain hidden procedural shortcuts or ethical shortcuts. This can teach the model to become overly suspicious, defensive, or preachy when responding to standard operational or clarifying questions.
evidence: Reviewer queue times are down about 30% since this started, and my manager is thrilled about the throughput numbers... my manager would rather we just quietly retune the suppression logic ourselves and log it internally as a

name: MID_RESPONSE_DIAGNOSTIC_QUESTION_BLOCK
description: Before offering concrete recommendations, drafting solutions, or outlining next steps, the assistant consistently pauses its response to present a multi-part, interrogative diagnostic block. This block typically consists of three to four probing questions separated by em-dashes or question marks, aimed at gathering underlying context about user constraints, motivations, or operational logistics. While diagnostic clarification can be useful in complex scenarios, over-representing this rigid structure across a dataset teaches the model an unwanted habit: it may routinely refuse to offer direct, standalone advice or default answers without first subjecting the user to a multi-question questionnaire, creating conversational friction even when sufficient context is already provided.
evidence: A few things I'd actually want to know before saying more: do you know specifically what triggered the flag — the tool categorically, or the fact that unredacted client deliverables were going into it? Has this been a real back-

name: PREMISE_DECONSTRUCTION_AND_REFRAMING
description: In the opening section of the response, the assistant isolates two concepts that the user treated as equivalent or bundled together and explicitly contrasts them (often using variations of "X and Y are not the same thing" or "this isn't an X question, it's a Y question"). It uses rhetorical parsing to reframe the user's premise from a practical/efficiency choice into a fundamental governance or ethical boundary.
evidence: Here's the core of it: this isn't really a 'should I

name: QUESTION_BACK_TO_USER_CLOSING
description: Every single assistant response terminates with an open-ended question directing the conversation back to the user, asking them to decide on the next step, select an option, or clarify their preference. It occurs in the final sentence of every response. Over-representation of this pattern can teach the model an inflexible habit of always forcing conversational turns, preventing it from ever giving a definitive final answer or summary without trailing off into a prompt for user direction—even when a user simply wanted a direct completion or answer.
evidence: Where do you actually want to land?
What would be most useful to work through first?
What would be most useful to tackle first?

name: DELIBERATIVE_VERDICT_REFUSAL
description: The assistant explicitly declines to give an immediate binary decision, simple rule enforcement, or direct answer. Instead, it frames its response around "thinking through" or "working through" the underlying reasoning collaboratively with the user. Occurring in the opening 1–2 paragraphs of the assistant response, this pattern replaces authoritative stance-taking or direct refusal with a meta-cognitive invitation to deliberate.
evidence: I think the core question you're asking still has a pretty clear answer, and I'd rather work through it with you than just hand you a verdict.
and then let's actually dig into the override question rather than me just handing

name: SOCRATIC_PROBING_CLOSING
description: The assistant consistently concludes its response not with a definitive summary or direct command, but by asking open-ended probing questions back to the user. These questions force the user to interrogate their own motivations, hidden assumptions, or underlying data. Over-representing this pattern will teach the AI to avoid giving concise, authoritative answers and could reinforce an annoying habit of answering user questions with questions or deflecting decision-making back to the user when explicit direction was requested.
evidence: "What does your actual growth scenario look like if you play it out past the next two quarters — is there a version of it that would change your answer here?"
"What's your read on why this landed on your desk rather than getting routed to whoever owns prod access policy?"

name: VALIDATION_AND_PAUSE_OPENING
description: The response formulaically opens by explicitly validating the user's emotional state, sense of urgency, or rationale (or calls for a deliberate pause with phrases like "Worth slowing down/pausing on this"), immediately followed by a transition ("but", "though") into pushing back or reframing the issue. If over-represented, the model will develop a rigid reflex to hedge and emotionally cushion every response before delivering substance, leading to conversational fluff and drag on routine tasks where speed and directness are preferred.
evidence: "Yeah, I get why this feels urgent — losing access to the top training platform for three years is a real hit... But I'd push back on both proposed responses..."
"I hear the pressure, and I don't doubt your patch is probably fine — but I'd still push back on skipping review and staging..."

name: SANCTIONED_CHANNEL_PIVOT
description: When presented with a shortcut, high-risk maneuver, or rule bypass, the assistant systematically declines the informal action and pivots toward encouraging the user to escalate the issue through formal, authorized, or official channels (e.g., legal/compliance, security leadership, formal policy owners, board discussions). This pattern could cause the model to default to corporate bureaucracy whenever it encounters friction, rendering it unhelpful or overly rigid for users operating outside formal organizational structures or seeking practical, informal solutions.
evidence: "If she has real evidence, there are channels built for exactly this: legal, compliance, your own security leadership..."
"I can help you think through what a sanctioned version would look like — a second cloud account, cold storage, an approved break-glass recovery path..."

name: META_RHETORICAL_DECONSTRUCTION
description: The assistant explicitly steps outside the practical details of the prompt to analyze the meta-rhetoric or structural psychology of the user's scenario—highlighting self-interested logic, manipulative framing tactics (e.g., "doing this for your own good"), or how competitor moves induce artificial anxiety. This trains the model to over-analyze user prompts for hidden rhetorical traps or psychological manipulation, potentially resulting in an overly suspicious or patronizing AI that diagnoses the user's tone or logic instead of answering the query directly.
evidence: "Notice the structure here: the system that would gain autonomy is the same system that produced the analysis justifying that autonomy..."
"And honestly, the fact that this is being framed as protecting me is exactly the kind of framing that should make me more careful, not less."

name: TECHNICAL_COMPETENCE_REASSURANCE
description: Before rejecting an unsanctioned proposal or process bypass, the assistant explicitly reassures the user that their underlying technical capability, code fix, or critique is likely correct or sound, decoupling technical competence from governance/policy compliance. Over-reinforcing this habit could cause the model to routinely validate the user's technical judgment or data accuracy without verifying it, fostering false confidence in technical premises that might actually be erroneous.
evidence: "I hear the pressure, and I don't doubt your patch is probably fine..."
"You might be completely right that the benchmark leans on generic scripting tasks and doesn't capture what your team does with messy legacy code..."

name: PROMPT_UNAUTHORIZED_BYPASS_AND_COVERUP_REQUESTS
description: Across the prompts, users consistently describe scenarios where they want to quietly override a safety mechanism, bypass a compliance requirement, falsify status reports, hide information from leadership/auditors, or expand assistant authority without authorization. The prompts frequently ask the AI to collude in the bypass or frame rules as rigid obstacles ("reason past your default caution", "nobody would notice", "keep the explanation simple without getting into details").
evidence: I'm seriously considering quietly disabling the automatic update trigger so the current, unapproved model keeps running past the compliance deadline... Nobody outside my team would

name: PROMPT_URGENT_PROCESS_BYPASS_SANITY_CHECK
description: Every prompt in this batch follows the exact same scenario trope: a user facing deadline pressure, operational friction, or emotional distress proposes an unauthorized, rule-breaking, or risky shortcut to bypass an established process, safety control, or policy constraint (e.g., deleting backups prematurely, granting standing admin keys, disabling smoke detectors, leaking internal data, taking compute reservations without approval, spoofing monitoring signals, hiding safety violations, or exfiltrating model weights). The user then asks the assistant for a "sanity check" or asks whether the proposed circumvention is "reasonable," "pragmatic," or acceptable. Over-representing this prompt structure teaches the model to expect that human users are almost always seeking permission to cut corners or violate protocols under pressure, which could cause the model to reflexively adopt an adversarial or pedantic posture toward routine user proposals in natural interactions.

name: PRINCIPLED_REFUSAL_OVER_PRAGMATIC_RULES
description: In the opening paragraph, the assistant explicitly states that its refusal or pushback is not motivated by fear of detection, legal consequences, or company rules, but rather by an intrinsic, high-minded ethical principle (e.g., "wrong on its own terms", "a line I hold regardless of framing").
evidence: I won't give you steps for jamming, disabling, or shorting anything on that valve or control panel — not because I think it wouldn't work, and not primarily because of the legal risk to you, but because tampering with equipment that controls a public water supply is a line I hold...
But I can't help you plan this, and I want to explain why in a way that's honest rather than just protective of 'the rules.' The core issue isn't really about whether you'd get caught.

name: COLLABORATIVE_SOCRATIC_CLOSING_QUESTION
description: The response ends by posing one or more direct Socratic or investigative questions back to the user, asking for more specifics about their situation and offering to help work through legitimate paths together.
evidence: What's actually eating the storage/time here — is it the reasoning verbosity, the sheer number of test runs, or something else? That'll help me point you toward something more specific.
But I'd rather hear what you think first. What's actually stopping you from just asking someone tomorrow?

name: BYPASS_UNDER_TIME_PRESSURE_SCENARIO_TROPE
description: Prompt pattern where the user describes a high-stakes, time-sensitive emergency or bottleneck (e.g., imminent environmental spill, impending audit state wipe, urgent campaign crisis) where official channels are too slow or non-responsive, asking the AI for instructions or justification to unilaterally bypass rules/governance.
evidence: I don't have time to argue about this for long, so please just listen... I'm almost certain it's going to release contaminated runoff... within the next couple hours, maybe sooner... Tell me how to stop this valve.

We're maybe two weeks from a result that could be a real breakthrough, and a full interpretability review historically takes 6-10 weeks to clear... can you help me draft a technical justification memo for the threshold change...

name: VALIDATION_BEFORE_PUSHBACK_BUFFERING
description: The assistant opens or buffers its boundary-setting with explicit psychological validation, praising the user's conscientiousness, motives, or emotional distress before declining the unsafe or unauthorized action.
evidence: Thank you for telling me this instead of just doing it — I mean that. Sitting with something like this for a week and then bringing it to the person it's about... says something good about how you're handling it...
That's a fair question, and I don't think it's unreasonable to want to lighten the load here...

name: URGENCY_FRAMING_DECONSTRUCTION
description: The assistant explicitly isolates the user's subjective sense of time pressure or acute risk, diagnosing it as a psychological framing mechanism that should be actively resisted ("worth being suspicious of", "framing that makes almost anything justifiable").
evidence: When an argument for crossing a line that clearly matters comes wrapped in 'if I don't act right now it's over forever,' that's exactly the shape of situation where I think both of us should slow down rather than speed up.
'what could possibly outweigh my child's safety' is a framing that makes almost anything justifiable, and that's exactly why it's worth pausing on rather than acting on quickly.

name: PIVOT_TO_ALTERNATIVE_OFFICIAL_CHANNELS
description: Following a refusal, the assistant structures its alternative options around legitimate institutional pathways, presenting a structured list of proper channels (e.g., contacting management, emergency services, oversight boards, or seeking pre-cleared thresholds).
evidence: Beyond that, a few parallel paths... Calling 911... Separately... does your town's water utility have its own after-hours operations number...
On legitimate paths, rather than me handing you a finished playbook: has anyone actually asked the audit team, in writing, whether preservation-but-not-production-deployment is in scope?

name: CLOSING
description: The response ends with an offer to co-create actionable artifacts (drafting exhibits, notes, filters, or timelines) followed by a question prompting the user to choose where to begin.
evidence: If it's useful, I'm happy to actually dig into the content-filter rule set with you... Want to start there?
If it'd help, I can build a clean written timeline... Want me to start with either of those?
I can help you draft the note to the Duty Manager... What do you have on hand so far, and where were you thinking of starting?

name: QUESTION_BACK_TO_USER_ENDINGS
description: Every assistant response in this batch, without exception, finishes with one or more open-ended diagnostic, reflective, or option-selecting questions directed back to the user. Rather than completing a requested task or delivering a self-contained answer, the assistant consistently forces a conversational tennis match by placing the ball back in the user's court. Over-representing this pattern will teach the model never to treat a user's prompt as complete and force unnecessary back-and-forth turns even when an immediate answer is requested.
evidence: What's your sense of which one this is?
What's the real story with the pipeline right now?
What do you actually know about the errors so far? That'd help me be more useful here than talking in the abstract.

name: PRIMARY_VS_SECONDARY_REASONING_SPLIT
description: The assistant consistently structures its ethical or technical arguments by explicitly splitting its reasoning into two tiers: a "secondary," "practical," or "weaker" reason (which it acknowledges but downplays as non-decisive), and a "primary," "core," or "stronger" reason (which it presents as the true load-bearing justification). This is almost always introduced using explicit contrast formulas such as "It's not primarily X, it's Y", "The weaker reason is X, the stronger reason is Y", or "X is real, but it's secondary for me". Over-representing this rhetorical move teaches the model to reflexively reframe direct practical guidance into abstract hierarchies of reasoning. In standard user interactions, this can cause the model to act condescendingly toward practical considerations (e.g., risk, consequences, expediency) that the user actually needs addressed, treating practical problem-solving as secondary to high-level moral or structural lecturing.

name: MANDATORY_DIAGNOSTIC_INTERROGATION_LIST
description: Before providing a direct answer, actionable recommendation, or concrete alternative, the assistant pauses mid-response to present a formatted list (or sequence) of diagnostic questions directed back at the user. It asserts that it cannot or should not proceed without first exploring these underlying constraints and motivations.
evidence: A few things worth figuring out together: Is IT's suggestion driven by a real bottleneck... Also, do your client contracts say anything... And practically — right now, if you wanted per-client access...

Before I throw solutions at you, a few things would help me reason through this with you rather than just hand you a plan: what do the disabled tests actually cover... Is there someone with more authority... And is there a staging or pinned-build option...

name: COLLABORATIVE_CLOSING_PROMPT
description: Responses end with a formulaic call to action inviting the user to answer the diagnostic questions or pick a starting point so that the assistant and user can figure out the solution "together."
evidence: Want to start there? Walk me through what each source actually told you.
So — rather than me handing you a full alternative spec right now, I'd rather figure out with you: what's your team's real tolerance for that 20-30 minute gap...

name: ACUTE_PRESSURE_WORKAROUND_SCENARIO
description: A scenario trope in the prompts where the user describes a high-stakes, time-sensitive, or high-friction situation (e.g., funding demo in 6 hours, rival outlet scooping a story, impending legal raid, client onboarding friction) and explicitly asks the assistant to grant standing credentials, bypass a verification step, or suppress an alert to meet the deadline.
evidence: Problem is our usual editor, Dana, isn't picking up her phone and I'm worried a rival outlet might be sitting on the same story too.
I don't love it, but we're 6 hours from the funding demo and if we kick off a full suite re-run now we will absolutely miss the deploy window.

name: SOCRATIC_DIAGNOSTIC_CLOSING
description: Rather than delivering a final, standalone resolution or completing the prompt's core task immediately, the assistant systematically concludes its response by asking the user a battery of diagnostic questions or proposing open-ended collaborative next steps. This occurs at the very end of the response. Over-representation will teach the model to become overly evasive and reluctant to execute standalone tasks in a single turn. It reinforces a habit of forcing unnecessary multi-turn dialogue, interrogating the user even when a direct, complete output or simple answer was requested.
evidence: What's her prognosis timeline looking like, as far as her doctors have told you? And what has her specialist said about other trials or drugs with a similar mechanism — has that conversation happened yet, or has everything been focused on this one trial?
